data.title: Kala Canggu is open
data.excerpt: Our first café outside Jakarta: a small brew bar five minutes from Berawa beach, open daily from 7am.
data.body:
After a year of planning, Kala Canggu opened its doors last Saturday. The space is small — twelve seats and a long brew bar — and the menu is short on purpose: espresso, filter, and whatever Nadia is experimenting with that week.

Come and say hello. The first filter is on us if you mention the Journal.

data.title: Why we roast lighter than you might expect
data.excerpt: Light doesn't mean sour. A short note from Sari on development, sweetness, and what we're actually aiming for.
data.body:
We get this question at the bar every week: why are your coffees so light? The honest answer is that we're chasing sweetness, and for the coffees we buy, sweetness lives in a narrower window than most people think.

Roast too dark and you replace the fruit with roast flavour. Roast too light and you get grassy, sour cups. Our job is to land in the middle, coffee by coffee.

data.title: Three days with the El Mirador producers
data.excerpt: Theo spent harvest week in La Plata with Lucía and Andrés Pardo. Notes on picking, fermentation tanks and the price of a good relationship.
data.body:
The road from Neiva to La Plata takes five hours and climbs most of the way. Finca El Mirador sits at the top of it, on a slope so steep that pickers tie their baskets to their waists.

We have bought from Lucía and Andrés for four harvests now. This year we went to talk about something less romantic than terroir: forward contracts, and how to make sure a good year at the farm is also a good year for the people who pick.

Fermentation, slowly

The Pardos ferment for 36 hours in shaded concrete tanks, much longer than their neighbours. It is the main reason their coffee tastes so clean, and the main reason we keep coming back.

data.title: Brewing guide: a sweeter V60 in four pours
data.excerpt: Our everyday pour-over recipe, written down at last. 15 g of coffee, 250 g of water, and a little patience.
data.body:
This is the recipe we use behind the bar for most light roasts. It is deliberately simple: four even pours, no stirring, and a total brew time around three minutes.

What you need

  • 15 g coffee, ground medium-fine

  • 250 g water just off the boil (93–95 °C)

  • A V60 02 and a rinsed paper filter

The pours

Bloom with 50 g and wait 40 seconds. Then pour to 100 g, 175 g and 250 g, waiting for the bed to drop a little between each pour. Aim to finish pouring by 1:45 and draining by 3:00.

If it tastes sour, grind finer. If it tastes bitter or dry, grind coarser. Change one thing at a time.

data.title: How we dial in a new Ethiopian lot
data.excerpt: From the first sample roast to the recipe printed on the bag: what happens in the week a new coffee arrives at the roastery.
data.body:
Every new coffee arrives at the roastery as a 300 g sample long before the full lot ships. That sample is where the real work happens: by the time sixty sacks land in Jakarta, we already know roughly how we want them to taste.

Three roasts, one table

We roast every sample three ways — fast, medium and long — and cup them side by side the next morning. Ethiopian naturals in particular can swing from jammy to vinegary in thirty seconds of development time, so the spread tells us where the edges are.

Most of the time the medium profile wins, and we spend the following week nudging it: a little more heat early to open up the fruit, a slightly longer finish when the acidity feels sharp.

Resting matters more than you think

Light-roasted naturals need time. We taste every roast at day 3, day 7 and day 14, and the recipe on the bag is based on day 10 — roughly when a bag ordered online is opened at home.

If a coffee tastes flat on day three, wait. If it still tastes flat on day ten, it's the roast.
